text: Netflix, Inc. is the world’s leading internet television network, serving over 117 million streaming memberships in more than 190 countries, with members watching over 140 million hours of TV shows and movies daily, including original series, documentaries, and feature films. Members can stream content anytime, anywhere, on nearly any internet-connected screen, with the ability to play, pause, and resume viewing without commercials or commitments. In the United States, members also receive DVDs delivered quickly to their homes. The company launched its streaming service in 2007 and has since built an ecosystem for internet-connected screens, expanding its content offerings to enhance consumer engagement. Its core strategy focuses on growing its streaming membership business globally while maintaining profit margin targets, by improving the member experience through expanded content—particularly original programming—and by enhancing the user interface and extending service availability to more devices. Members can download selected titles for offline viewing. Netflix began its international expansion in Canada in 2010 and has since launched services globally, excluding The People's Republic of China and territories where U.S. companies are not permitted to operate. The company operates in three reportable segments: Domestic streaming, International streaming, and Domestic DVD. Domestic streaming generates revenue from monthly membership fees for streaming content in the United States, International streaming from streaming content outside the U.S., and Domestic DVD from DVD-by-mail services. As of December 31, 2017, Netflix had approximately 5,500 total employees, of which about 5,400 were full-time, including around 600 temporary workers. The company was incorporated in Delaware in August 1997 and completed its initial public offering in May 2002. Its principal executive offices are located at 100 Winchester Circle, Los Gatos, California 95032, and its telephone number is (408) 540-3700. The company maintains a website at www.netflix.com, which is not incorporated into this report. It makes available, free of charge, its Annual Reports on Form 10-K, Quarterly Reports on Form 10-Q, Current Reports on Form 8-K, and amendments to those reports as soon as reasonably practicable after filing with the Securities and Exchange Commission. Material financial information is also shared through the investor relations website (http://ir.netflix.com), SEC filings, press releases, public conference calls, and webcasts, with social media posts potentially considered material. As of June 30, 2017, the aggregate market value of voting stock held by non-affiliates of the registrant, based on the closing sales price of its common stock on the NASDAQ Global Select Market, was $54,917,149,461. Shares beneficially owned by each executive officer, director, and any person known to beneficially own 10% or more of the outstanding common stock have been excluded from this calculation because such individuals may be considered affiliates. This determination of affiliate status is not binding for any other purpose. As of January 25, 2018, there were 433,948,461 shares of the registrant’s common stock, par value $0.001, outstanding. The company competes in a highly competitive and rapidly changing entertainment video market against multichannel video programming distributors (MVPDs), internet-based content providers (including those offering pirated content), video gaming providers, and DVD retailers, as well as against other entertainment sources. It competes for content both through licensed streaming and original programming. The company aims to capture "moments of truth" when consumers choose its service over alternatives, improving its technology and content—especially exclusive and curated original programming—to achieve this. Membership growth shows a seasonal pattern, with the first and fourth quarters (October through March) historically seeing the highest growth in both domestic and international streaming. This pattern is increasingly influenced by the release of high-profile original content. Internationally, seasonal trends are expected to become more predictable as the service becomes more established. Netflix considers its trademarks, service marks, copyrights, patents, domain names, trade dress, trade secrets, and proprietary technologies to be vital to its success and protects them through a combination of legal measures and confidentiality agreements. However, the company cannot guarantee it will prevail in any intellectual property disputes. The company is a well-known seasoned issuer and is not required to file reports under Section 13 or 15(d) of the Securities Exchange Act of 1934. It has filed all required reports during the prior 12 months and has been subject to such filing requirements for the past 90 days. It has submitted and posted electronically all required Interactive Data Files. The registrant has not elected to use the extended transition period for complying with new or revised financial accounting standards. The registrant is not a shell company. The document includes forward-looking statements regarding business strategy, financial performance, membership growth, content investments, competition, and risks, which are subject to uncertainties and risks that could cause actual results to differ materially. A detailed discussion of these risks is included in Item 1A: "Risk Factors."

The entertainment video market is highly competitive and rapidly evolving, with consumers having increasing access to content through various distribution channels that operate under subscription, transactional, ad-supported, or piracy-based models. Piracy poses a significant threat due to its appeal of offering virtually all content for free, leading to rapid global growth and challenging traditional providers such as broadcasters, cable operators, and internet-based entertainment companies. These established competitors benefit from long operating histories, large customer bases, strong brand recognition, and substantial financial, marketing, and operational resources, enabling them to secure favorable supplier terms, adopt aggressive pricing, and invest heavily in product development, technology, infrastructure, content acquisition, and marketing. New entrants or existing providers may introduce unique services or business combinations to strengthen their positions. If the company fails to compete effectively or profitably, it could suffer adverse effects on market share, revenues, and profitability. The company’s content commitments—typically multi-year agreements with studios and content providers, including non-cancelable talent agreements—are characterized by fixed costs not tied to membership usage or size, and are included in the Contractual Obligations section and related financial notes. These long-term, fixed commitments may limit operational flexibility and negatively impact liquidity and results of operations if membership growth or revenue does not meet expectations. Content produced directly by the company often requires larger upfront cash payments than other licensed content, further straining cash flow. If content is not well received by consumers or cannot be shown in certain territories, the company may face difficulties in acquiring or retaining members, and due to the fixed nature of these commitments, it may not be able to quickly adjust its content offerings. As a producer and distributor, the company faces risks of liability for negligence, copyright or trademark infringement, or claims related to marketing materials. The expansion of original programming—such as TV series and movies—is intended to differentiate the service, enhance the brand, and attract members, but if such programming fails to meet expectations in terms of cost, viewing, or popularity, the business, brand, and operations could be harmed. The company also bears production risks, including completion and talent risks, and may face increased costs or delays due to changes in collective bargaining agreements. If the company creates or licenses merchandise based on original programming, it could face product liability, intellectual property, or other claims. Content may be removed from the service or production discontinued if it is not well received or could damage the brand. Failure to anticipate costs or mitigate risks—such as content not being used or being removed—could harm the business, and litigation to defend claims could be costly and damaging to operations. The company may not be indemnified or fully insured against such claims. If studios or rights holders refuse to license content on acceptable terms, the company’s ability to offer streaming content will be compromised, and costs could rise. Certain licenses allow rights holders to withdraw content quickly, and as competition increases, programming costs may rise. The company focuses on securing exclusive rights and maintaining a cost-efficient, compelling mix of content, and if the mix fails to delight members, membership acquisition and retention could suffer. Music and performance rights require licenses from collection management organizations (CMOs); failure to reach mutually acceptable terms could lead to litigation or injunctions, and ongoing disputes among CMOs could result in rights being unilaterally withdrawn, increasing costs or limiting content availability. The company’s international expansion involves managing diverse content, cultural practices, legal environments, and consumer behaviors, and faces risks such as staffing challenges, political instability, compliance with U.S. and local laws, regulatory actions, weaker intellectual property protections, tax changes, currency fluctuations, profit repatriation restrictions, differing payment systems, censorship, low device penetration, data protection laws, broadband availability, integration challenges, and more lenient views on piracy. Failure to manage these risks could harm international operations and overall business performance. The company is subject to taxation in multiple U.S. and foreign jurisdictions, requiring significant judgment in assessing global tax positions, with potential for reversal by tax authorities and increased obligations due to new laws or changes in interpretation, including recent U.S. tax reform and EU or OECD tax proposals. Changes in how the company markets its service—such as curtailment of marketing channels due to rising costs or perceived brand damage—could reduce member acquisition and increase marketing expenses. Partnerships with cable, satellite, and telecommunications providers are essential for delivering content via set-top boxes and mobile devices; if these partnerships expire or are not renewed on acceptable terms, or if partners fail to update devices, service delivery and member retention could be harmed. Devices are manufactured by third parties, and performance issues or consumer dissatisfaction with the connection between devices and the service could lead to claims or reputational damage. Cybersecurity risks—including cyber-attacks, denial of service, data breaches, and unauthorized access—pose a threat to the reliability and security of the company’s systems and those of third parties, potentially resulting in service disruptions, data loss, intellectual property theft, and reputational harm. The company has implemented safeguards but has experienced unauthorized data releases in the past. The reliability and security of its systems are critical to maintaining member trust and service availability.

Interruptions in computer systems or internet access could make the service unavailable, degraded, or hinder the delivery of streaming content or DVD selections, reducing the appeal of the membership service to current and potential members. The company’s computer systems and those of third parties are vulnerable to cybersecurity risks, including cyber-attacks from state-sponsored or individual actors such as computer viruses, denial of service attacks, and physical or electronic break-ins, which may lead to service disruptions, data or intellectual property loss, misuse, or theft. Although the company has implemented systems and processes to prevent such attacks, unauthorized releases of digital content assets have occurred, though they have not had a material impact to date. There is no guarantee that future attacks would not have a material effect, and the company’s insurance does not cover expenses related to such disruptions or unauthorized access. Preventing such intrusions is costly and may limit service functionality or negatively impact the service offering. Any significant disruption to service or access to systems could result in lost memberships and harm business operations. The company uses its own communications and computer hardware, either in its facilities or through third-party web hosting providers, and also relies on third-party cloud computing services, including Amazon Web Services (AWS), which provides a distributed computing infrastructure. The company has architected its software and systems to utilize AWS, currently running the vast majority of its computing on AWS, and due to the lack of easy alternatives, any disruption to AWS would adversely impact operations. While Amazon competes in retail, the company does not believe AWS use would give Amazon a competitive advantage. If the technology used in operations fails, is unavailable, or underperforms, business and operational results could be negatively affected. The company uses a mix of proprietary and third-party technology for content recommendations, merchandising, and content delivery, including its own content delivery network (CDN); however, if ISPs do not interconnect with the CDN or if the CDN operates poorly, streaming delivery could be impaired. Similarly, if recommendation technology fails to predict or suggest content members will enjoy, member acquisition and retention could suffer. Third-party technology used for marketing, payments, and daily operations, if it fails or operates improperly due to software bugs, could impair service delivery and member retention. Harm to members’ personal devices from software used in operations could also negatively affect business outcomes. Changes in government regulations related to the internet or other business areas could require business model changes or increase operating expenses. As the company expands internationally, governments are introducing or extending regulations related to broadcast media and tax, and consumer protection laws may become stricter, imposing additional burdens. Laws affecting net neutrality, such as those implemented in the European Union or recently repealed in the U.S., create uncertainty, and network operators may engage in discriminatory practices that could impede growth or increase costs. If network operators block, restrict, or impair access to the service, or implement usage-based pricing, bandwidth caps, or tiered access, the company could face higher expenses and reduced membership acquisition and retention. Network operators, who also provide multichannel video programming, have incentives to treat their own data preferentially, which could harm the company’s growth, especially if such discriminatory practices are implemented. Privacy concerns may limit the company’s ability to collect and use membership data, and disclosures of such data could damage reputation and lead to legal claims. The company collects and uses member data, including billing data, stored on its own systems and third-party systems, with encryption and authentication used to protect billing data like credit card numbers. Despite these measures, unauthorized intrusions into member or employee data could occur, leading to reluctance from members to provide necessary information, legal claims, regulatory fines, or reputational harm. The company is subject to payment processing risk, relying on internal and third-party systems to process payments via credit/debit cards, gift cards, direct debit, and online wallets, subject to rules, fees, and regulations. Disruptions, increased fees, changes in the payment ecosystem, delays in payments, or regulatory changes could harm revenue and operating expenses. In some cases, the company uses cable and other partners to bill subscribers; if these partners stop processing payments, alternative collection methods would be needed, negatively affecting member acquisition and retention. Fraudulent use of payment methods could also impact results and damage consumer perception. If trademarks and other proprietary rights are not adequately protected, brand value and competitive position could decline, and competitors might mimic the service. The company relies on confidentiality agreements, licenses, and legal protections such as trademarks, copyrights, patents, and trade secrets, and has filed trademark and patent applications. However, these may not be approved, third parties may challenge existing rights, or infringement may occur, requiring costly legal actions or changes to business practices. The company holds domain names like Netflix.com, and failure to protect them could harm brand reputation and user access. Third parties may acquire similar domain names, which could be costly or impossible to prevent. Intellectual property claims, including from third parties alleging infringement, could be expensive and result in loss of rights to websites, streaming technology, recommendation systems, content selection, or marketing. The company uses third-party intellectual property in content creation and marketing, and disputes could require costly litigation, diversion of personnel, removal of content, development of non-infringing technology, or changes to content, merchandising, or marketing. Legal proceedings, including copyright, patent, consumer, and securities class actions, are costly and time-consuming, potentially leading to content unavailability, service disruptions, and diversion of management attention. The company may seek additional capital through equity, equity-linked, or debt securities due to negative operating cash flows over the past three years, primarily from investments in original streaming content. If capital is raised through equity, stockholders may experience dilution, and new securities could have rights senior to common stockholders, potentially negatively impacting the stock price. The company has substantial indebtedness and obligations, including $6.5 billion in senior notes as of December 31, 2017, a $500 million unsecured revolving credit facility (with no borrowings as of that date), and approximately $7.5 billion in total content liabilities, not including significant streaming content commitments not yet recognized as liabilities. This debt and obligation burden may make it difficult to meet financial obligations, limit borrowing capacity, restrict cash flow use, reduce flexibility in responding to business changes, place the company at a competitive disadvantage, and increase vulnerability to economic downturns. Streaming content obligations are long-term and multi-year, so the company may not be able to reduce them in response to economic downturns or reduced cash flow, potentially forcing access to capital markets at unfavorable times, which could negatively affect the stock price.

This Annual Report on Form 10-K highlights that the company’s substantial indebtedness and other obligations, including long-term streaming content commitments, may hinder its ability to meet financial obligations such as scheduled principal and interest payments on its Notes and other debts. These obligations could limit the company’s capacity to borrow funds for working capital, capital expenditures, acquisitions, or general business purposes, restrict the use of cash flow or access to additional financing, require a significant portion of operating cash flow to be allocated to debt service and other obligations, reduce flexibility in responding to business or industry changes, place it at a competitive disadvantage compared to less leveraged competitors, and increase vulnerability to adverse economic or industry conditions. The streaming obligations are large and multi-year, so the company cannot reduce them in the near term during an economic downturn or decline in operating cash flow, potentially forcing it to access the capital markets at an unfavorable time, which could negatively impact its stock price. The company may not generate sufficient cash to service its debt and other obligations, as payment ability depends on financial and operating performance, which is influenced by economic, competitive, and uncontrollable factors. Over the past three years, cash flows from operating activities have been negative, and the company may not achieve sufficient positive cash flow to meet debt and streaming obligations. If cash flows are insufficient and refinancing or restructuring is not possible on commercially reasonable terms, the company could face substantial liquidity issues, leading to delays or reductions in investments and capital expenditures, or the need to sell material assets or operations—measures that may not be feasible on satisfactory terms or at all, and could materially and adversely affect its business, operations, or financial condition. The company relies on the continued service of key personnel, including its Chief Executive Officer and co-founder Reed Hastings, and executive team members, and faces significant competition in hiring and retaining skilled employees, which could disrupt operations. The Domestic DVD segment is experiencing a decline in memberships, and although the company believes this segment will continue to generate significant contribution profit, a faster-than-anticipated decline could harm the business. The company does not plan to increase resources or improve technology for DVD operations, and service interruptions or degradations could lead to increased member cancellations and reduced satisfaction. If the U.S. Postal Service increases delivery rates or implements service reductions, such changes could negatively affect customer satisfaction and the segment’s contribution profit. The company’s charter documents and Delaware law include provisions that may discourage, delay, or prevent a takeover that shareholders might consider favorable, such as the ability to issue up to 10,000,000 shares of undesignated preferred stock without shareholder approval, a classified board, restrictions on written consent, advance notice requirements for shareholder proposals, and prohibitions on calling special meetings. Delaware law also prevents a business combination with a shareholder owning 15% or more of the stock unless the shareholder has held it for three years or the board approves the transaction, and such a merger could trigger retention payments to executives under the Amended and Restated Executive Severance and Retention Incentive Plan, increasing transaction costs. The company’s stock price has been highly volatile due to factors such as variations in operating results, analyst expectations, business announcements, competition, market volatility, demand for the stock, and competitor performance, and investors may not be able to resell shares at or above their original purchase price. Following periods of volatility, the company has faced securities litigation, which may continue and result in substantial costs and management distraction. Financial forecasting requires management judgments and estimates, which may differ materially from actual results, including estimates of content asset usage and amortization periods; revisions to these estimates could lead to impairment charges or increased expenses, causing the company to miss earnings guidance or negatively impact reported results and stock price. The company’s corporate headquarters are located in Los Gatos, California, with approximately 600,000 square feet of leased space, and it leases additional offices in the U.S., including about 400,000 square feet in Los Angeles, California for content acquisition, marketing, and administrative functions, and in Fremont, California for DVD operations, as well as office space in other countries to support international streaming. The company believes its current facilities are adequate and that suitable additional or substitute space will be available as needed. Information on legal proceedings is included in Note 5, Commitments and Contingencies in the financial statements. The company’s common stock is traded on the NASDAQ Global Select Market under the symbol “NFLX.” As of January 25, 2018, there were approximately 327 stockholders of record, though there are many more beneficial owners. The company has not declared or paid any cash dividends and has no current intention to do so. The selected financial data for the years ended December 31, 2017 through 2013 shows revenues of $11,692,713 in 2017, increasing from $8,830,669 in 2016 to $6,779,511 in 2015, with operating income rising to $838,679 in 2017 from $379,793 in 2016, and net income reaching $558,929 in 2017. Earnings per share were $1.29 (basic) and $1.25 (diluted) in 2017, with weighted-average common shares outstanding of 431,885 (basic) and 446,814 (diluted). Net cash (used in) provided by operating activities was negative at $1,785,948 in 2017, compared to $1,473,984 in 2016, and free cash flow was $2,019,659 in 2017. Cash, cash equivalents, and short-term investments totaled $2,822,795 as of December 31, 2017, and total content assets, net, were $14,681,989. Working capital was $2,203,662 in 2017, and total assets were $19,012,742. Long-term debt was $6,499,432, and non-current content liabilities were $3,329,796, resulting in total content liabilities of $7,502,837. Total stockholders’ equity was $3,581,956 as of December 31, 2017. The data has been adjusted for the company’s seven-for-one stock split that occurred in July 2015.

As of December 31, 2017, Netflix had 117,582 global streaming memberships, an increase of 25% from 93,796 in 2016 and 25% from 74,762 in 2015. Net global streaming membership additions during the period were 23,786 in 2017, up from 19,034 in 2016 and 17,371 in 2015. Global streaming average monthly revenue per paying membership was $9.43 in 2017, up 10% from $8.61 in 2016 and 6% from $8.15 in 2015. Consolidated revenues for the year ended December 31, 2017, were $11,692,713, a 32% increase from $8,830,669 in 2016 and a 30% increase from $6,779,511 in 2015. International revenues accounted for 44% of consolidated revenue in 2017, up from 36% in 2016. The revenue growth was driven by membership growth, particularly in international memberships, which accounted for 49% of total average paid streaming memberships as of December 31, 2017, up from 43% in 2016. The increase in operating income was due to higher revenues, partially offset by increased content expenses, including a $39.1 million expense related to abandoned unreleased content, and higher headcount costs for streaming service improvements, international expansion, and content production. Net income increased 199% to $558,929 in 2017 from $186,678 in 2016 and 52% from $122,641 in 2015, primarily due to higher operating income and a tax benefit from the adoption of ASU 2016-09 in the first quarter of 2017, partially offset by higher interest expense from increased notes outstanding and foreign exchange losses from remeasuring euro-denominated senior notes. Netflix offers three membership plans: basic (standard definition, one screen), standard (high definition, two screens), and premium (high and ultra-high definition, four screens). Pricing in the U.S. ranged from $7.99 to $13.99 per month for basic to premium, and internationally from approximately $4 to $20 per month (U.S. dollar equivalent). In the Domestic streaming segment, memberships at the end of 2017 were 54,750, up 11% from 49,431 in 2016 and 10% from 44,738 in 2015. Paid memberships were 52,810 in 2017, up 10% from 47,905 in 2016 and 10% from 43,401 in 2015. Average monthly revenue per paying membership was $10.18 in 2017, up 11% from $9.21 in 2016 and 8% from $8.50 in 2015. Revenues were $6,153,025 in 2017, up 21% from $5,077,307 in 2016 and 21% from $4,180,339 in 2015. Cost of revenues increased by $463,441 (16%) and $368,596 (15%) respectively, primarily due to a $419.0 million increase in content amortization and $44.4 million in other costs. Marketing expenses rose by $170,499 (45%) and $65,186 (21%), mainly due to increased advertising and partner payments. Contribution margin improved to 37% in 2017 from 36% in 2016 and 33% in 2015. In the International streaming segment, memberships at the end of 2017 were 62,832, up 42% from 44,365 in 2016 and 48% from 30,024 in 2015. Paid memberships were 57,834 in 2017, up 40% from 41,185 in 2016 and 50% from 27,438 in 2015. Average monthly revenue per paying membership was $8.66 in 2017, up 11% from $7.81 in 2016 and 4% from $7.48 in 2015. Revenues were $5,089,191 in 2017, up 58% from $3,211,095 in 2016 and 64% from $1,953,435 in 2015. Cost of revenues increased by $1,226,541 (42%) and $1,130,995 (64%), primarily due to a $990.3 million increase in content amortization and $236.2 million in other costs. Marketing expenses rose by $116,445 (19%) and $101,800 (20%). Contribution profit increased by $535.1 million to $226,589 in 2017 from a loss of $308,521 in 2016 and $333,386 in 2015, with a contribution margin of 4% in 2017, up from (10)% in 2016 and (17)% in 2015. The increase in international revenues was due to a 43% growth in paid memberships and an 11% increase in average monthly revenue per paying membership, with foreign exchange fluctuations reducing revenues by approximately $21.9 million in 2017 compared to 2016. In 2016, international revenues grew 57% in paid memberships and 4% in average revenue per paying membership, with foreign exchange unfavorably impacting revenues by approximately $174.0 million. Cost of revenues increased by $998.5 million in 2016 due to content expenses and $132.5 million in other costs, partially offset by exchange rate fluctuations. Marketing expenses increased due to higher advertising and partner payments. The International streaming segment's contribution profit improved significantly due to profitability in mature markets offsetting investments in new markets.

The increase in international revenues was driven by a 57% growth in the average number of paid international memberships and a 4% increase in average monthly revenue per paying membership, which resulted from price changes and plan mix, partially offset by unfavorable foreign exchange rate fluctuations. The company estimates that international revenues would have been approximately $174.0 million higher in the year ended December 31, 2016 if foreign exchange rates had remained consistent with those in the year ended December 31, 2015. If foreign currency exchange rates fluctuate beyond expectations, revenues and average revenue per paying membership may differ from projections. The increase in international cost of revenues was primarily due to a $998.5 million rise in content expenses related to existing and new streaming content, including more exclusive and original programming, and a $132.5 million increase in other costs, mainly from higher streaming delivery expenses, customer service call center costs, and payment processing fees, all driven by a growing member base, partially offset by exchange rate fluctuations. International marketing expenses rose due to expenses for territories launched in the last eighteen months. International contribution losses decreased by $24.9 million year over year as growth in paid memberships and revenue outpaced marketing spending growth. In the Domestic DVD segment, net losses were $(731) thousand in 2017 compared to $(790) thousand in 2016 and $(863) thousand in 2015, with a 7% decrease in memberships at the end of the period and an 18% decline in memberships from 2016 to 2017, and a 16% decline from 2015 to 2016. Paid memberships declined by 17% from 2016 to 2017 and 16% from 2015 to 2016. Average monthly revenue per paying membership decreased by $0.05 from 2016 to 2017 and by $0.08 from 2015 to 2016. Revenues declined by $91,770 thousand (17%) from 2016 to 2017 and by $103,470 thousand (16%) from 2015 to 2016. Cost of revenues decreased by $60,217 thousand (23%) and $61,166 thousand (19%) respectively, leading to a $31,553 thousand (11%) decrease in contribution profit, with contribution margin rising to 55% in 2017 from 52% in 2016 and 50% in 2015, due to reduced DVD usage and lower content expenses. Technology and development expenses increased to $1,052,778 thousand in 2017 from $852,098 thousand in 2016 and $650,788 thousand in 2015, representing a 24% and 31% increase respectively, with a 9% share of revenues in 2017 compared to 10% in 2016 and 2015. The increase was primarily due to a $131.1 million rise in personnel-related costs, including stock-based compensation, from higher employee compensation and a 3% headcount growth to support streaming improvements and international expansion, plus $39.1 million in third-party expenses (cloud computing) and $30.1 million in facilities-related costs, mainly for the expanded Los Gatos, California headquarters. General and administrative expenses rose to $863,568 thousand in 2017 from $577,799 thousand in 2016 and $407,329 thousand in 2015, an increase of 49% and 42% respectively, with a 7% share of revenues in both 2017 and 2016, up from 6% in 2015. The increase was due to a $184.7 million rise in personnel-related costs, including stock-based compensation, from a 56% headcount increase to support international expansion and original content production, and higher compensation for existing employees, plus $49.9 million in facilities-related costs from new Los Angeles, California facility and expanded Los Gatos headquarters, and $49.4 million in third-party expenses (contractors and consultants). Interest expense increased to $238,204 thousand in 2017 from $150,114 thousand in 2016 and $132,716 thousand in 2015, a 59% and 13% increase respectively, with a 2% share of revenues each year. The increase in 2017 was primarily due to higher long-term debt, with $229.2 million in interest on notes. Interest and other income (expense) decreased to $115,154 thousand in 2017 from $30,828 thousand in 2016 and $31,225 thousand in 2015, a 474% and 199% decrease respectively, primarily due to foreign exchange losses. In 2017, the $127.9 million foreign exchange loss was mainly from a $140.8 million loss in remeasuring €1,300 million Senior Notes, partially offset by gains from remeasuring cash and content liabilities in other currencies. In 2016, interest and other income (expense) increased by $62,053 thousand due to foreign exchange gains, primarily from remeasuring significant content liabilities in currencies other than functional currencies. The provision for income taxes decreased to $73,608 thousand in 2017 from $73,829 thousand in 2016 and $19,244 thousand in 2015, a 200% and 284% decrease respectively, with an effective tax rate of (15)% in 2017, 28% in 2016, and 14% in 2015. The decline in the effective tax rate was due to excess tax benefits from adopting ASU 2016-09 and increased foreign income taxed at rates below the U.S. statutory rate, with a $243.5 million difference between the 15% rate and the 35% federal statutory rate in 2017, partially offset by state taxes and non-deductible expenses and the provisional impact of tax law changes. On December 22, 2017, the Tax Cuts and Jobs Act was enacted, which reduced the corporate tax rate from 35% to 21% for tax years beginning after December 31, 2017, transitioned U.S. international taxation to a territorial system, and imposed a one-time transition tax on the deemed repatriation of foreign earnings as of December 31, 2017. The company recorded $79.1 million in additional income tax expense in the fourth quarter of 2017, including a $46.9 million provisional adjustment for deferred tax assets and liabilities based on expected reversal rates, and a $32.2 million provisional adjustment for the one-time transition tax on $484.9 million in foreign earnings. A $66.5 million benefit was also recorded for foreign taxes expensed in prior years that may now be claimed as foreign tax credits, based on sufficient projected foreign source income. The effective tax rate increased in 2016 to 28% from 14% in 2015, mainly due to a $13.4 million release of tax reserves in 2015 and higher foreign taxes, with a $17.3 million difference between the 28% rate and the 35% federal statutory rate in 2016, primarily due to Federal and California R&D credits, partially offset by state income taxes, foreign taxes, and non-deductible expenses. Cash and cash equivalents and short-term investments increased by $1,089.0 million in the year ended December 31, 2017 to $2,822,795 thousand from $1,733,782 thousand in 2016, primarily due to cash received from debt issuance, partially offset by increased cash used in operations. As of December 31, 2017, foreign subsidiaries held $611.3 million in cash and cash equivalents. The Tax Cuts and Jobs Act included a one-time transition tax on unremitted foreign earnings, resulting in a $32.2 million tax expense recorded in 2017. Long-term debt, net of debt issuance costs, increased by $3,135.1 million due to €1,300.0 million note issuances in May 2017 and $1,600.0 million in October 2017. The earliest maturity date for outstanding long-term debt is February 2021. In July 2017, the company entered into a $50 million agreement.

As of December 31, 2017, cash and cash equivalents held by our foreign subsidiaries amounted to $611.3 million. The Tax Cut and Jobs Act of 2017 included a one-time transition tax on unremitted foreign earnings, and as a result, we recorded a tax expense of $32.2 million related to the transition tax on the one-time mandatory deemed repatriation of all our foreign earnings as of that date. Long-term debt, net of debt issuance costs, increased by $3,135.1 million due to long-term note issuances of €1,300.0 million in May 2017 and $1,600.0 million in October 2017. The earliest maturity date for our outstanding long-term debt is February 2021. In July 2017, we entered into a $500.0 million unsecured revolving credit facility (“Revolving Credit Agreement”), with an uncommitted incremental facility to increase the amount by up to an additional $250.0 million subject to certain terms and conditions. As of December 31, 2017, no amounts had been borrowed under the Revolving Credit Agreement. We anticipate financing our capital needs in the debt market, as we believe our after-tax cost of debt is lower than our cost of equity. Our ability to obtain additional financing will depend on, among other things, our development efforts, business plans, operating performance, and the condition of the capital markets at the time we seek financing.
